notes.text: A great multitude — Of those who had happily finished their course. Such multitudes are afterwards described, and still higher degrees of glory which they attain after a sharp fight and magnificent victory, chap. xiv, 1; xv, 2; xix, 1; xx, 4. There is an inconceivable variety in the degrees of reward in the other world. Let not any slothful one say, "If I get to heaven at all, I will be content:" such an one may let heaven go altogether. In worldly things, men are ambitious to get as high as they can. Christians have a far more noble ambition. The difference between the very highest and the lowest state in the world is nothing to the smallest difference between the degrees of glory. But who has time to think of this? Who is at all concerned about it? Standing before the throne - In the full vision of God. And palms in their hands - Tokens of joy and victory.

Salvation to our God — Who hath saved us from all evil into all the happiness of heaven. The salvation for which they praise God is described, verse 15; that for which they praise the Lamb, verse 14; and both, in the sixteenth and seventeenth verses. ver. 16, 17

And all the angels stood — In waiting. Round about the throne, and the elders and the four living creatures - That is, the living creatures, next the throne; the elders, round these; and the angels, round them both. And they fell on their faces - So do the elders, once only, chap. xi, 16. The heavenly ceremonial has its fixed order and measure.

Amen — With this word all the angels confirm the words of the "great multitude;" but they likewise carry the praise much higher. The blessing, and the glory, and the wisdom, and the thanksgiving, and the honour, and the power, and the strength, be unto our God forever and ever - Before the Lamb began to open the seven seals, a sevenfold hymn of praise was brought him by many angels, chap. v, 12. Now he is upon opening the last seal, and the seven angels are going to receive seven trumpets, in order to make the kingdoms of the world subject to God. All the angels give sevenfold praise to God.

And one of the elders — What stands, verses 13-17, ver. 13-17 might have immediately followed the tenth verse; but that the praise of the angels, which was at the same time with that of the "great multitude," came in between. Answered - He answered St. John's desire to know, not any words that he spoke.

My Lord — Or, my master; a common term of respect. So Zechariah, likewise, bespeaks the angel, Zech. i, 9; iv, 4; vi, 4. Thou knowest - That is, I know not; but thou dost. These are they - Not martyrs; for these are not such a multitude as no man can number. But as all the angels appear here, so do all the souls of the righteous who had lived from the beginning of the world. Who come - He does not say, who did come; but, who come now also: to whom, likewise, pertain all who will come hereafter. Out of great affliction - Of various kinds, wisely and graciously allotted by God to all his children. And have washed their robes - From all guilt. And made them white - In all holiness. By the blood of the Lamb - Which not only cleanses, but adorns us also.

Therefore — Because they came out of great affliction, and have washed their robes in his blood. Are they before the throne - It seems, even nearer than the angels. And serve him day and night - Speaking after the manner of men; that is, continually. In his temple - Which is in heaven. And he shall have his tent over them - Shall spread his glory over them as a covering.
Neither shall the sun light on them — For God is there their sun. Nor any painful heat, or inclemency of seasons.

For the Lamb will feed them — With eternal peace and joy; so that they shall hunger no more. And will lead them to living fountains of water - The comforts of the Holy Ghost; so that they shall thirst no more. Neither shall they suffer or grieve any more; for God "will wipe away all tears from their eyes."

glossa.text: *After these things.* When he had seen, according to the figure, those to be marked out under a certain number, and only from the children of Israel, now he openly teaches that by that number all the faithful, and by the twelve tribes all the nations, are to be understood. *Standing.* Namely, ready to obey God the judge, or their prelates also. This in the present.
*Salvation to our God who sitteth.* Not through ourselves, but through the Lamb do we have salvation, that is, the remission of sins, and good working, and eternal glory.

*And all.* By the angels spoken of above, the greater prelates can be understood; by these, the lesser prelates, or subjects only, as there are angels and archangels, and yet all are angels, that is, messengers. But even now there are greater and lesser prelates, that is, archbishops and bishops.

*Amen.* As if he should say: If you attribute it to God, you do well. Or *amen* will be read with what follows: *Amen,* that is, truth in the things premised, and *benediction,* that is, the exaltation which he has above every creature, or our exaltation in the virtues: and *brightness,* that is, impassibility, or yours in works.
*And one answered.* The multitude having been seen in so great dignity, he is moved to consider by what way it was able to ascend thither, that he may teach others to look upon the same.
*Their robes,* etc. The innocence received in baptism, or their bodies.
*They shall not hunger, nor thirst,* etc. He who gave knowledge to the angels will give the same knowledge to them also.

*He shall lead them to the fountains of the waters of life,* etc. And by this he shall lead them in time to come to refreshment of every kind. *God shall wipe away every tear.* Every grief, whether for their own offences, or for adversities, or exile, or other things of this sort.

notes.text: Shall boast — Shall glory in this, that I have so powerful and so gracious a master. The humble - The righteous.
Together — Not in place, for David was now banished from the place of God's publick worship, but in affection: let our souls meet, and let our praises meet in the ears of the all-hearing God.
Lightened — Comforted and encouraged. Ashamed - They were not disappointed of their hope.
This man — David.
The angel — The angels, the singular number being put for the plural.
O taste — Make trial, of it by your own experience of it. Good - Merciful and gracious.
Fear — Reverence, serve, and trust him: for fear is commonly put for all the parts of God's worship.

glossa.text: *I will bless.* ((CASS.)) The second psalm through an imperfect alphabet, etc., *as far as* he is glorified together with him.

*In the Lord shall my soul be praised.* ((ID.)) For his own praise is the preaching of his Lord, as a good servant glories in the good repute of his lord. *The meek.* Not the learned, not those who fast, because they are proud: but the meek, because they have temperance in all things. The meek, not being proud of their own understanding; not bearing the yoke of God after the manner of the untamed.

*O magnify the Lord.* Spiritual grace does not wish to do alone what profits many; whence it calls others: *Magnify,* that it might draw those invited, it tells what goods came to it thereby: *I sought the Lord. Out of all.* It cannot be told piecemeal how great things he obtained who sought nothing other than God. *Come ye.* ((CASS.)) Now piecemeal he admonishes the saints concerning the new countenance. As if to say, *Magnify:* and if among the first, come ye into what is pleasant. Or, *Magnify,* and in what order? behold: *Come ye* by faith. ((AUG.)) Come ye by cleaving with faith, and by running with the two feet of a twin charity. ((CASS.)) The praises being set first, he exhorts to communion. *Let them not be confounded.* ((AUG.)) Whatever happens here to the just man, he does not blush, because he is always the higher with God: but the proud man blushes in adversities, because he has not drawn near to God.

*The poor man.* ((CASS.)) *This one* is here the spiritual man, because he draws near and is enlightened, and shall not blush; because, when he cries out, he is freed from all the straits of the world at his death, when he now passes over to God.

*He shall send in an Angel. Come ye,* and as this poor man cried out and was heard, in the same way *he shall send in an Angel,* etc. ((AUG.)) *He shall send in an Angel.* Other interpreters have rendered it thus: *The Angel of the Lord surroundeth in a ring them that fear him.* An Angel from heaven, or a man, who is a minister of the will of God. Faulty codices have it. *The Lord shall send in an Angel.*

*Taste and see.* Here openly of the sacrament which he bore in his hands. *Taste* the flesh and blood of Christ. *The Lord is sweet.* ((ID.)) And delightful: because he is life to him that takes him, driving away all troubles in the world to come, that is: Hope through this for eternal life. ((CASS.)) And because God is life, the flesh which he united to himself is life-giving.

*All ye his saints.* ((CASS.)) No one, however well deserving, shall leave off from this, let him not presume upon security. *For.* ((AUG.)) The Lord was feeding him that despised him, and he will forsake him that fears him. But he promises not superfluous things, but necessary ones. *There is no want.* Because even in the present they have as much as nature requires.

*The rich have wanted and have suffered hunger.* ((CASS.)) Because they have not faith. *They have suffered hunger,* because they are not filled with the body of the Lord. For what have they who have not God? Or, *the rich have wanted,* that is, they shall lack the highest good, although they hunger, that is, desire. But those who seek with their whole zeal shall have without diminution the good which is every good.

notes.text: That we should be called — That is, should be, the children of God. Therefore the world knoweth us not - They know not what to make of us. We are a mystery to them.

It doth not yet appear — Even to ourselves. What we shall be - It is something ineffable, which will raise the children of God to be, in a manner, as God himself. But we know, in general, that when he, the Son of God, shall appear, we shall be like him - The glory of God penetrating our inmost substance. For we shall see him as he is - Manifestly, without a veil. And that sight will transform us into the same likeness.
And every one that hath this hope in him — In God.

glossa.text: *See,* etc. Consider diligently with how great and what manner of gifts God has shown his fatherly charity toward us. For he granted that in this world we should be named sons of God in name and in deed, and that in the world to come we should be so, by possessing the inherited blessedness. *He gave.* To this end God gave charity, that we might know how to love him and be able to, yet not as servants a master, but as sons a father. Whence it is said: *And as many as received him, he gave them power to be made the sons of God ((Joan. I))*.

*We are the sons of God.* As if he should say: To be and to be called sons of God, what dignity is that? he answers: *Dearly beloved, now we are the sons of God.* Now through the miracles which we do and through purity of life it appears that we are sons of God, but whatever is in the present is little in comparison with what is to come. *We shall be like to him.* For when we shall fully enjoy the contemplation of the unchangeable and eternal Godhead, we also shall be immortal and eternal in him: not indeed the same as he, but like, because we are a creature and were made to his likeness. *Because we shall see.* According as the Word was made flesh, the wicked have seen him, and in the judgment they shall see him: but how the Word in the beginning was with the Father, the just alone shall see: the wicked man shall be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.
*He sanctifieth himself. ((BEDA.))* He does not take away free will, when he says, etc., *as far as* saying to God: *Thou art my helper, forsake me not ((Psal. XXVI))*.

notes.text: And seeing the multitudes — At some distance, as they were coming to him from every quarter. He went up into the mountain - Which was near: where there was room for them all. His disciples - not only his twelve disciples, but all who desired to learn of him.

And he opened his mouth — A phrase which always denotes a set and solemn discourse; and taught them - To bless men; to make men happy, was the great business for which our Lord came into the world. And accordingly he here pronounces eight blessings together, annexing them to so many steps in Christianity. Knowing that happiness is our common aim, and that an innate instinct continually urges us to the pursuit of it, he in the kindest manner applies to that instinct, and directs it to its proper object. Though all men desire, yet few attain, happiness, because they seek it where it is not to be found. Our Lord therefore begins his Divine institution, which is the complete art of happiness, by laying down before all that have ears to hear, the true and only true method of acquiring it. Observe the benevolent condescension of our Lord. He seems, as it were, to lay aside his supreme authority as our legislator, that he may the better act the part of: our friend and saviour. Instead of using the lofty style, in positive commands, he, in a more gentle and engaging way, insinuates his will and our duty, by pronouncing those happy who comply with it.

Happy are the poor — In the following discourse there is,

1. A sweet invitation to true holiness and happiness, ver. 3-12.

2. A persuasive to impart it to others, ver. 13-16.

3. A description of true Christian holiness, ver. 17; chap.vii, 12. (in which it is easy to observe, the latter part exactly answers the former.)

4. The conclusion: giving a sure mark of the true way, warning against false prophets, exhorting to follow after holiness. The poor in spirit - They who are unfeignedly penitent, they who are truly convinced of sin; who see and feel the state they are in by nature, being deeply sensible of their sinfulness, guiltiness, helplessness. For theirs is the kingdom of heaven - The present inward kingdom: righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost, as well as the eternal kingdom, if they endure to the end. Luke vi, 20.

They that mourn — Either for their own sins, or for other men's, and are steadily and habitually serious. They shall be comforted - More solidly and deeply even in this world, and eternally in heaven.

Happy are the meek — They that hold all their passions and affections evenly balanced. They shall inherit the earth - They shall have all things really necessary for life and godliness. They shall enjoy whatever portion God hath given them here, and shall hereafter possess the new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness.
They that hunger and thirst after righteousness — After the holiness here described. They shall be satisfied with it.

The merciful — The tender-hearted: they who love all men as themselves: They shall obtain mercy - Whatever mercy therefore we desire from God, the same let us show to our brethren. He will repay us a thousand fold, the love we bear to any for his sake.
The pure in heart — The sanctified: they who love God with all their hearts. They shall see God - In all things here; hereafter in glory.

The peace makers — They that out of love to God and man do all possible good to all men. Peace in the Scripture sense implies all blessings temporal and eternal. They shall be called the children of God - Shall be acknowledged such by God and man. One would imagine a person of this amiable temper and behaviour would be the darling of mankind. But our Lord well knew it would not be so, as long as Satan was the prince of this world. He therefore warns them before of the treatment all were to expect, who were determined thus to tread in his steps, by immediately subjoining, Happy are they who are persecuted for righteousness' sake. Through this whole discourse we cannot but observe the most exact method which can possibly be conceived. Every paragraph, every sentence, is closely connected both with that which precedes, and that which follows it. And is not this the pattern for every Christian preacher? If any then are able to follow it without any premeditation, well: if not, let them not dare to preach without it. No rhapsody, no incoherency, whether the things spoken be true or false, comes of the Spirit of Christ.

For righteousness' sake — That is, because they have, or follow after, the righteousness here described. He that is truly a righteous man, he that mourns, and he that is pure in heart, yea, all that will live godly in Christ Jesus, shall suffer persecution, 2 Tim. iii, 12. The world will always say, Away with such fellows from the earth. They are made to reprove our thoughts. They are grievous to us even to behold. Their lives are not like other men's; their ways are of another fashion.
Revile — When present: say all evil - When you are absent.
Your reward — Even over and above the happiness that naturally and directly results from holiness.

glossa.text:
*And Jesus seeing. ((AUG.))* With this Luke agrees, saying: *And it came to pass in those days, he went out into a mountain to pray ((Luc. VI))*, etc. But Luke says, etc., *as far as* for not all men can do all things: which is thought the truer, although the same [sermon] of both may be seen to have been delivered at once.

*He went up.* Teaching his own to go up and not to remain in the crowd: being about to teach a higher righteousness than that which is of the Scribes and the Pharisees. He himself, a mountain, went up into a mountain, that he might teach the higher summits of the virtues, and might show that the Church, above which he sits preaching, is to be raised more loftily by the Lord's precept, which the same teaching would more fully instruct unto the end of the world. He leads the apostles apart more eminently, that from the mountain the mountains may first receive peace for the people. *He was set down.* The sitting is of the humanity, by which he is known. Whence: *And the world knew him not,* before the incarnation. *They came.* That they may hear the nearer, who hasten in mind to fulfil.

*And opening.* The opening of the mouth signifies the depth of the sacrament. He opened as it were an abyss, as it were a treasure, as it were a river of paradise. On this mountain he writes the New Testament in the hearts of sons, beginning from beatitude, who on mount Sinai gave the Old Testament on stones to servants, beginning from terror.

((AUG.)) The sermon which our Lord spoke on the mountain, as in the Gospel, etc., *as far as, Everyone who hears these my words and shall do them, I will liken him to a wise man ((Matth. VII))*.

*Blessed. ((GREG. NYSS.))* Beatitude, as my opinion carries it, is the comprehension of all those things which, etc., *as far as* for misery is a wretchedness in bitter and sorrowful chances and calamities that do not fall out by our own will.

*Blessed are the poor.* The number of the sentences is to be diligently attended to. For beatitude begins from humility.

*((HIER.)) Blessed are the poor in spirit.* Because it is not necessity but faith, and the devotion of poverty, that makes men blessed, etc., *as far as* as the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, so poverty is the beginning of beatitude.

((CHRYSOST.)) The poor in spirit are the humble and contrite of heart. And by spirit he here means the soul and the will. But because many are humble not of their own accord, but constrained by necessity, he calls the first sort blessed.

*Blessed are the meek.* The meek are those who master evil habits: perfect virtue is the possession of one's habits.

 ((THEOPH.)) The meek are not those who are not angry at all, etc., *as far as* so the doctrine of a man is discerned through patience.

*They shall possess the land. ((AUG.))* That land I believe to be the one of which it is said in the Psalm: *Thou art my hope, my portion in the land of the living ((Psal. CLXI))*.

*Blessed are they that mourn.* For their own sins or for others', which mourning is from the lower watering, but that which comes from the upper watering is out of desire for the heavenly country. The one washes present filth, the other kindles more sharply the lovers of eternal things. But he who has laid down his sins, has corrected his habits by meekness, and has wept besides, can now hunger and thirst after righteousness, which before he could not. This virtue is not fulfilled without the spirit of fortitude: because through him, by hungering, we shall one day come to fulness. *Blessed are they that mourn.* It remains, after the things aforesaid, to purge by mourning the foulness of our ruins. Mourning for sins or out of heavenly desire earns consolation, and no other does.

These are enlightened by the spirit of knowledge, that they may know in what evils they are wrapped.

((HILAR.)) For those that mourn, not for those grieving over bereavements, or insults, or losses, but for those weeping over their old sins, and made wretched by the consciousness of the crimes with which we are befouled, this assiduous consolation is prepared in heaven.

*Blessed are they that hunger.* Lovers of the good word, to whom it is not enough that they are just, but they always thirst for the work of righteousness.

Righteousness is to render to each his own, to oneself, and to one's neighbors, and to God. This righteousness will not be fully fulfilled until God be all in all: therefore here we can hunger, not be filled. The light of righteousness is mercy, the strength of mercy is righteousness; this mercy has need of the spirit of counsel, without which no one is merciful with circumspection. The beginning is to have mercy on oneself, the end is to die for another. For the order of showing mercy is that each man begin from himself. Christ hints at the end, having died out of mercy for sinners.

*Blessed are the merciful.* Mercy is born of the things that go before, because if true humility has gone before, and the mind grows meek, and weeps for its own falls and others', and hungers after righteousness, afterwards true mercy is born. For then it will make others' miseries its own and will help according to its powers: and if the means of helping is wanting, compassion will not be wanting: *Be ye merciful as your Father also is merciful ((Luc. VI))*, that is, let us have mercy unto that end unto which God also has mercy, that goodness may overflow upon all: mercy without righteousness is called remission and lukewarmness; righteousness without mercy is called severity and harshness.

*Blessed are the peacemakers. ((RAB.))* The peacemakers are those who compose all the motions of the mind and subject them to reason, because nothing resists those who are like the Father, etc., *as far as* but when God shall be all in all, then the beatitude of adoption will be given.

*Blessed are they that suffer persecution.* In the seven aforesaid there is the showing and the proving of perfection. Those who have the aforesaid things can suffer persecution: and he rightly holds the aforesaid things which he has received who is ready to die for them.

*Blessed are you when they shall revile you.* Thus far he set down his sentences generally, as though to those absent, although they belonged to those present also, now he turns his words to them (although this belongs to others also), foretelling how great things they should suffer for his name: because he wished to make known to them the dignity of their rank, saying: *You are the salt of the earth, you are the light of the world;* that from the sad things they might take humility, from the glad things consolation.

*Shall revile.* The ancient translation has: *When men shall hate you, and shall say all that is evil, and shall cast you out.* Yet the sense is the same in ours, since revilings come from hatred of the heart. He who chooses the glory of heaven does not fear reproach on earth; as much as each man rejoices at the praise of men, so much does he grieve at reproach. Him whom praise lifts up, blame casts down: where a man seeks to be praised only before God, he does not fear to be confounded in the sight of men. *Lying.* He adds this, lest he glory of whom evil things are truly said. He adds also: *For my sake,* because sometimes false things are said, which comes about through the rashness of men, yet they do not suffer this for Christ's sake, whom they do not follow.

*For your reward is very great in heaven.* Not in rolling things, since an eternal reward ought not to be in rolling things, but in spiritual firmaments, where everlasting righteousness dwells. Already therefore they feel this reward who rejoice in spiritual goods. But it will be made perfect when this mortal shall put on immortality. *For so they persecuted,* etc. He tempers the rigor of the passion by an example. Persecution is made in three ways: by hatred of the heart, by words, by deeds.

hymns.title: Fix me for my long white robe
See that host all dressed in white
Victim Divine, thy grace we claim
Deck thyself, my soul, with gladness
Come, ye disconsolate, where'er ye languish
When peace, like a river, attendeth my way

praise.title: Yet Not I But Through Christ in Me

echoes.text: Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So will your seed be.”
echoes.note: The Abrahamic promise: "count the stars, if you are able to count them... so shall your offspring be" — the uncountable, innumerable seed. John's "a great multitude, which no man could count" (hon arithmesai auton oudeis edynato) directly fulfills the count-if-you-can promise, now extended beyond Israel to every nation. Strong on volume and on John's larger Abrahamic-fulfillment logic (the multitude completes what the sealed 144,000 represent).

echoes.text: I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth, so that if a man can number the dust of the earth, then your seed may also be numbered.
echoes.note: Parallel Abrahamic promise: offspring "as the dust of the earth, which if a man can number..." — the explicit "if a man can number" idiom that John negates ("which no man could count"). LXX ei dynatai tis exarithmesai is verbally close to John's clause. Pairs with Gen 15:5 as the twin innumerability promises being eschatologically realized.

echoes.text: You shall take on the first day the fruit of goodly trees, branches of palm trees, and boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook; and you shall rejoice before Yahweh your God seven days.
echoes.note: The palm branches (phoinikes) in the multitude's hands evoke the Feast of Tabernacles/Sukkot, where worshipers take "branches of palm trees" and rejoice before the LORD — fitting the booth/tabernacle imagery that immediately follows (7:15, God spreading his tabernacle, skenosei). Festal-joy and ingathering-harvest coherence is strong; the specific lulav connection is the principal reason this is an allusion not a mere echo.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: "all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him" (Aram./Theod. laoi, phylai, glossai) — Daniel's stereotyped fourfold list of the nations is the template for John's recurrent "every nation, tribe, people, and language" formula (cf. Rev 5:9; 13:7). The multitude drawn from all peoples fulfills Daniel's universal dominion of the Son of Man. Recurrence in Revelation strengthens the link.

echoes.text: And he entered into it on the three and twentieth day of the second month, in the hundred and seventy and first year, with praise and palm branches, and with harps, and with cymbals, and with viols, and with hymns, and with songs: because a great enemy was destroyed out of Israel.
echoes.note: Simon's triumphal entry into the Jerusalem citadel "with praise and palm branches (baia)... and with hymns and songs" — Second-Temple precedent for palm branches as the gesture of victory celebration and deliverance, illuminating why the redeemed multitude (victors out of tribulation) bear palms while acclaiming salvation. Confirms the victory-procession nuance alongside the Tabernacles nuance (cf. also 2 Macc 10:7; John 12:13).

echoes.text: Salvation belongs to Yahweh. Your blessing be on your people. Selah.
echoes.note: "Salvation belongs to the LORD" (LXX Ps 3:9, tou kyriou he soteria) — the acclamation "Salvation be to our God" closely mirrors this psalmic confession that deliverance is God's alone. Idiom is common across the Psalter (cf. Ps 37:39; Jonah 2:9), so attribution to a single verse is uncertain, but the verbal shape is closest here.

echoes.text: Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head above all.
echoes.note: David's doxology — "Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory... and the majesty... blessing" — a sevenfold-style ascription of attributes to God that stands behind the seven-membered doxology of 7:12 (blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, power, might). Liturgical-doxological coherence; faint as a specific citation since such ascriptions are formulaic.

echoes.text: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”
echoes.note: The throne-vision with surrounding heavenly beings prostrate/crying praise underlies the angels, elders, and four living creatures falling before the throne; the living creatures themselves derive from Isa 6 seraphim and Ezek 1/10. Faint here because the throne-room cast is established earlier (Rev 4) rather than newly drawn from Isaiah in this verse.

echoes.text: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun strike them: for he who has mercy on them will lead them, even by springs of water he will guide them.
echoes.note: "They shall not hunger nor thirst, neither scorching heat nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them" — the densest verbal source in the chapter. John reproduces all four elements in order: no hunger, no thirst, no sun/scorching heat smiting them, and a shepherd-guide leading to springs of water. Hays' criteria max out (volume, recurrence of the Servant-shepherd motif, coherence with the new-exodus ingathering). LXX peinasousin... dipsesousin... kausön... pegas hydaton tracks John closely.

echoes.text: He has swallowed up death forever! The Lord Yahweh will wipe away tears from off all faces. He will take the reproach of his people away from off all the earth, for Yahweh has spoken it.
echoes.note: "He will swallow up death forever, and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces" — direct source for "God will wipe away every tear from their eyes" (exaleipsei... pan dakryon). The eschatological consolation at the victory-banquet on the mountain. High verbal volume; recurs at Rev 21:4. Note the MT "swallow up death" vs. LXX katepien ho thanatos ischysas; John follows the tear-wiping clause closely regardless of the textual divergence in the first colon.

echoes.text: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd.
echoes.note: "I will set up over them one shepherd... my servant David, and he shall feed them and be their shepherd" — the messianic Davidic-shepherd promise underlying "the Lamb... shepherds them." Striking oxymoron (the Lamb is the Shepherd) fuses Ezekiel 34's shepherd-king with John's Lamb-Christology. Strong coherence; Ezek 34:23 cited as the principal verse of the chapter-long shepherd oracle.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.
echoes.note: "The LORD is my shepherd... he leads me beside still waters" (LXX Ps 22:1-2, hodegesen me epi hydatos anapauseos) — the shepherd-leads-to-water image directly behind "shepherds them, and leads (hodegesei) them to springs of life-giving waters." John's hodegeo echoes the psalm's verb. High volume and coherence with the Isa 49 / Ezek 34 shepherd cluster.

echoes.text: Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine; he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes.
echoes.note: Judah's blessing: "he washed his garments in wine and his robe in the blood of grapes" — the only OT image of washing a robe in (grape-)blood, giving John the paradoxical "washed their robes... white in the Lamb's blood." Coheres with the Judah/Lion-Lamb Christology and ties pericope 7.4 back to the Judah-first tribal list (7.2). The blood-of-grapes/blood-of-the-Lamb figural link is medium-to-strong on coherence though contested on verbal volume.

echoes.text: “Come now, and let us reason together,” says Yahweh: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. Though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
echoes.note: "Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow" — the prophetic image of sin-cleansing producing whiteness underlies robes "made white" through the Lamb's blood (cleansing-unto-whiteness). Coheres with the purification motif; medium volume since John supplies the paradoxical agent (blood) absent from Isaiah.

echoes.text: Many shall purify themselves, and make themselves white, and be refined; but the wicked shall do wickedly; and none of the wicked shall understand; but those who are wise shall understand.
echoes.note: "Many shall purify themselves and make themselves white (LXX leukanthosin) and be refined" through the time of trouble — the closest source for the eschatological making-white of the faithful precisely amid tribulation, matching "made them white" of those who "came out of the great tribulation." Daniel's end-time-refining-whitening is thematically and verbally apt (leukaino).

echoes.text: Some of those who are wise shall fall, to refine them, and to purify, and to make them white, even to the time of the end; because it is yet for the time appointed.
echoes.note: "Some of the wise shall stumble, to refine and purify them and to make them white (LXX leukanai), until the time of the end" — companion to Dan 12:10; the wise are whitened/refined through persecution. Reinforces the tribulation-purification reading of the white-robed multitude. Cited alongside 12:10 as the Danielic whitening pair.

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book.
echoes.note: "there shall be a time of trouble (LXX thlipsis / Theod. hemera thlipseos) such as never has been" — the eschatological great distress that John names "the great tribulation" (tes thlipseos tes megales). Daniel supplies the technical term and the deliver-the-named-remnant frame; coherent with the sealing/deliverance arc of the whole chapter.

echoes.text: I will set my tent among you, and my soul won’t abhor you. I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.
echoes.note: "I will make my dwelling (LXX skenen) among you... and I will walk among you" — the covenant-presence/tabernacling promise behind "He who sits on the throne will spread his tabernacle (skenosei) over them." Part of the dwelling-of-God-with-his-people stream (Ezek 37:27; cf. Rev 21:3). Medium coherence; the skene cognate strengthens it.

echoes.text: My tent also shall be with them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
echoes.note: "My dwelling place (LXX kataskenosis) shall be with them, and I will be their God" — the eschatological tabernacling-with-the-redeemed promise, near-synonymous with Lev 26:11 and directly echoed in the skenoo of 7:15 (and again Rev 21:3). Reinforces the new-covenant-presence reading.

echoes.text: Yahweh will create over the whole habitation of Mount Zion, and over her assemblies, a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night; for over all the glory will be a canopy. There will be a pavilion for a shade in the daytime from the heat, and for a refuge and for a shelter from storm and from rain.
echoes.note: Over Zion a canopy/booth (LXX skepe) for "shade from the heat" and shelter — combines the tabernacle-spread-over-them and the no-scorching-heat motifs in a single Zion-protection oracle, paralleling 7:15-16. Faint but apposite; possibly part of the cluster behind John's protective-canopy imagery.

echoes.text: Yahweh is your keeper. Yahweh is your shade on your right hand. The sun will not harm you by day, nor the moon by night.
echoes.note: "The LORD is your keeper... the sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night" — the sun-shall-not-strike-you protection paralleling "neither will the sun beat on them." Idiomatically close but likely mediated through Isa 49:10, which John follows more fully; cited as a secondary witness.

echoes.text: Seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying, “We will eat our own bread, and wear our own clothing: only let us be called by your name. Take away our reproach.”
echoes.note: Faint: white-garment/clean-robe symbolism of the purified Zion-remnant in Isa 4 (the branch made glorious, the survivors called holy) coheres with the white-robed survivors of tribulation; included as a contested ingathering-of-the-holy-remnant resonance rather than a verbal source.

echoes.text: “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
echoes.note: "the fountain of living waters" (LXX pegen hydatos zoes) — Jeremiah's image of God as the living-water source colors "springs of life-giving waters" (pegas hydaton zoes); the phrase also runs through Ps 36:9, Zech 14:8, and John 4/7. Common idiom, so single-verse attribution is uncertain; cited as the closest verbal match.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)
Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: You are the children of Yahweh your God. You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.
echoes.note: Israel addressed as 'children of the LORD your God' grounds John's astonishment that believers 'should be called children of God.' The divine-sonship status, once Israel's covenant identity, is here extended to the community. John intensifies the relation with the language of bestowed love.

echoes.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
echoes.note: Hosea promises that those who were 'not my people' will be called 'children of the living God,' the precise idiom of being 'called children of God.' This eschatological renaming of the people supplies John's vocabulary for present sonship. The passage was a standard locus for adoption-into-sonship.

echoes.text: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”
echoes.note: God tells Moses no one may see his face and live, the canonical statement of the unseen God. John's hope that 'we will see him just as he is' deliberately reverses this prohibition as eschatological promise. The tension between present hiddenness and future sight is structured by this Exodus limit.

echoes.text: As for me, I shall see your face in righteousness. I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with seeing your form.
echoes.note: The psalmist hopes to 'behold your face in righteousness' and be 'satisfied with your likeness' upon awaking, the classic beatific-vision text and a likeness motif. John's 'we will be like him, for we will see him' closely mirrors this seeing-and-likeness pairing. The awaking imagery resonates with eschatological revelation.

echoes.text: I will tell the north, ‘Give them up!’ and tell the south, ‘Don’t hold them back! Bring my sons from far, and my daughters from the ends of the earth—
echoes.note: God commands the gathering of 'my sons' and 'my daughters' from the ends of the earth, framing the people as God's children. The verse reinforces the sonship motif John applies to believers. Faint but congruent with the divine-family theme.

echoes.text: After my skin is destroyed, then in my flesh shall I see God, Whom I, even I, shall see on my side. My eyes shall see, and not as a stranger. “My heart is consumed within me.
echoes.note: Job hopes that after his skin is destroyed he will 'see God' with his own eyes, an early witness to seeing God beyond death. This undergirds John's confidence that the not-yet-revealed future includes seeing him. The contested textual history of the verse makes the echo suggestive rather than certain.

echoes.text: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
echoes.note: Moses uniquely beholds the form/likeness of the LORD, an exceptional clear sight of God amid general hiddenness. John universalizes such direct vision as the believers' destiny. A faint background to seeing him 'as he is.'

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Moses went up to God, and Yahweh called to him out of the mountain, saying, “This is what you shall tell the house of Jacob, and tell the children of Israel:
echoes.note: Jesus 'went up onto the mountain' to teach Torah, evoking Moses ascending Sinai to receive the law; Matthew presents a new-Moses giving authoritative instruction from a mountain.

echoes.text: But the humble shall inherit the land, and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace.
echoes.note: 'The gentle/meek shall inherit the earth/land' is a near-verbatim echo of LXX Ps 36:11 (Ps 37:11), the clearest single source behind the third beatitude.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound; to proclaim the year of Yahweh’s favor, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all who mourn; to appoint to those who mourn in Zion, to give to them a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of […]
echoes.note: Isaiah's anointed proclaims good news to the poor and comfort to all who mourn; multiple beatitudes (poor, mourning-comforted, righteousness) cluster on this Servant text, which Jesus elsewhere claims.
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind; to declare the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of recompence; to comfort all that mourn; that there should be given to them that mourn in Sion glory instead of ashes, the oil of joy to the mourners, the garment of glory for the spirit of heaviness: and […]

echoes.text: Who may ascend to Yahweh’s hill? Who may stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.
echoes.note: 'Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? ... He who has clean hands and a pure heart' — direct source for 'blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.'

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Come up to me on the mountain, and stay here, and I will give you the stone tablets with the law and the commands that I have written, that you may teach them.”
echoes.note: Moses summoned up the mountain to receive the tablets of law and commandment; the Sermon's mountain setting figurally recasts the giving of Torah.

echoes.text: Moses called to all Israel, and said to them, “Hear, Israel, the statutes and the ordinances which I speak in your ears this day, that you may learn them, and observe to do them.”
echoes.note: Moses assembles and teaches Israel the statutes; the seated Teacher addressing disciples mirrors the Mosaic instruction frame.

echoes.text: For thus says the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.
echoes.note: God dwells with the contrite and lowly in spirit; 'poor in spirit' draws on this prophetic ideal of humble dependence on God.

echoes.text: For all these things has my hand made, and so all these things came to be,” says Yahweh: “but to this man will I look, even to him who is poor and of a contrite spirit, and who trembles at my word.
echoes.note: God regards the poor, contrite in spirit, who tremble at his word — background for 'blessed are the poor in spirit.'

echoes.text: Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.
echoes.note: The LORD is near the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit; coheres with poor-in-spirit and those who mourn.

echoes.text: Instead of your shame you shall have double; and instead of dishonor they shall rejoice in their portion: therefore in their land they shall possess double; everlasting joy shall be to them.
echoes.note: The mourners shall possess a double portion and everlasting joy; reinforces the inheritance/reward logic of the beatitudes.

echoes.text: Surely God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart.
echoes.note: 'God is good to the pure in heart' — recurrent Psalter theme behind the sixth beatitude.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
echoes.note: 'Blessed is the man...' — the makarism/beatitude form itself is rooted in the Psalter's wisdom blessing formula.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: 'I desire mercy'; the mercy-receives-mercy logic of the fifth beatitude resonates with Hosea, a text Matthew cites twice elsewhere.

echoes.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: To do justice, love mercy (hesed), walk humbly — clusters mercy, righteousness, and humility that pervade the beatitudes.

echoes.text: As for me, I shall see your face in righteousness. I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with seeing your form.
echoes.note: 'I shall behold your face in righteousness' — beatific seeing of God promised to the pure in heart.

echoes.text: But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.
echoes.note: The saints of the Most High receive and possess the kingdom; underwrites 'theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven' (bracketing beatitudes 1 and 8).

echoes.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
echoes.note: 'You are children of the living God' — divine-sonship language behind 'they shall be called children of God.'

echoes.text: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.
echoes.note: 'Seek peace and pursue it'; the active peacemaking blessed in the seventh beatitude.

echoes.text: but they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and scoffed at his prophets, until the wrath of Yahweh arose against his people, until there was no remedy.
echoes.note: Israel mocked and persecuted the prophets; basis for 'so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.'

echoes.text: “Listen to me, you who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is my law; don’t fear the reproach of men, neither be dismayed at their insults.
echoes.note: 'Fear not the reproach of men' addressed to those with God's law in their heart — close parallel to being reproached/reviled for righteousness' sake.

echoes.text: But let us lie in wait for the righteous man, Because he is of disservice to us, And is contrary to our works, And upbraids us with sins against the law, And lays to our charge sins against our discipline. He professes to have knowledge of God, And names himself servant of the Lord. He became to us a reproof of our thoughts. He is grievous to us even to behold, Because his life is unlike other men’s, And his paths are of strange fashion. We were accounted […]
echoes.note: The wicked plot against the righteous one, reproaching and persecuting him to test his patience; Second Temple background for the persecuted-righteous beatitudes.

echoes.text: Blessed is he whose disobedience is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man to whom Yahweh doesn’t impute iniquity, in whose spirit there is no deceit.
echoes.note: Beatitude-form blessing ('Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven'); shapes the genre of Jesus' blessings.

echoes.text: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun strike them: for he who has mercy on them will lead them, even by springs of water he will guide them.
echoes.note: The redeemed 'shall not hunger nor thirst'; background for 'hunger and thirst after righteousness ... shall be filled.'

echoes.text: Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted in them. Then they cried to Yahweh in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses, he led them also by a straight way, that they might go to a city to live in. Let them praise Yahweh for his loving kindness, for his wonderful works to the children of men! For he satisfies the longing soul. He fills the hungry soul with good.
echoes.note: God satisfies the hungry and thirsty soul; coheres with the fourth beatitude's promise of being filled.

echoes.text: He who despises his neighbor sins, but blessed is he who has pity on the poor.
echoes.note: 'Blessed is he who is generous/merciful to the poor'; wisdom background for 'blessed are the merciful.'

echoes.text: Jacob called the name of the place Peniel: for, he said, “I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.”
echoes.note: Jacob saw God face to face and lived; background to the extraordinary promise 'they shall see God.'

echoes.text: The kingdom and the dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky, shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.
echoes.note: Kingdom and dominion given to the people of the holy ones; reinforces the kingdom-inheritance frame.

echoes.text: Didn’t you, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel, and give it to the seed of Abraham your friend forever?
echoes.note: Israel as God's 'children'/friends; background for peacemakers 'called children of God.'

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Elijah laments the slaying of the prophets; the persecuted-prophets motif of v.12.

echoes.text: There was also a man who prophesied in Yahweh’s name, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath Jearim; and he prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah: and when Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men, and all the princes, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death; but when Uriah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt: and Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, Elnathan the son […]
echoes.note: The prophet Uriah killed for prophesying; concrete instance of persecuted prophets behind v.12.

echoes.text: Also there arose Elijah the prophet as fire, And his word burned like a torch: Who brought a famine upon them, And by his zeal made them few in number. By the word of the Lord he shut up the heaven: Thrice did he thus bring down fire. How was you glorified, O Elijah, in your wondrous deeds! And who shall glory like to you? Who did raise up a dead man from death, And from the place of the dead, by the word of the Most High: Who brought down kings to […]
echoes.note: Elijah among the persecuted prophets; deuterocanonical recollection of the prophets' suffering invoked in v.12.

echoes.text: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.
echoes.note: Those who sow in tears reap with joy; coheres with mourners being comforted and rejoicing.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you.
echoes.note: Deuterocanonical exhortation to mercy/almsgiving that obtains divine favor; background to 'blessed are the merciful.'

registers.label: Spare
lines: A great multitude no one could number stands before the throne.
Robed in white, with palms in their hands.
These are the ones who have come through the great ordeal.
God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.
We join our voices with the saints and angels.
Taste and see that the Lord is good.
Come, let us worship with the whole company of heaven.
We come, with all the saints. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Imagine a crowd too vast to count, from every nation and language, robed in white, palm branches lifted, the whole company of the redeemed around one throne.
Blessing and honor and glory to our God!
There stand the ones we loved and lost, the saints who came through the great ordeal, hungry no more, thirsty no more, every tear wiped dry.
Blessing and honor and glory to our God!
And we are already his children, though what we shall be has not yet appeared; we shall see him and be like him.
Blessing and honor and glory to our God!
Taste and see that the Lord is good; blessed are the poor, the mourning, the meek, for theirs is the kingdom.
Blessing and honor and glory to our God!
So lift your voice with the great multitude and worship.
Blessing and honor and glory to our God! Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: A multitude no one can number stands before the throne.
With all the saints, we worship.
They have come through the great ordeal; God wipes every tear.
With all the saints, we worship.
We are God's children now, and shall be like him.
With all the saints, we worship.
Come, join the whole company of heaven.
We come, with all the saints. Amen.
